lesson_overview.x03: Game Deconstruction and Scratch Environment Setup

learning_outcomes.x08:
WA8DIGDI1: Design the user experience (UX) of a digital system.
WA8DIGDTID1: Investigate a problem for a given need or opportunity.
WA8DIGDTPM1: Plan, develop and communicate, using project management processes, considering time, resources and costs to achieve solutions.
WA8DIGDTDE1: Design processes and solutions considering a range of technologies and techniques, using appropriate technical terms.
x09: Identify at least three independent components of a digital game (Bat sprite, Crystal sprite, Score variable) by applying the computational thinking strategy of Decomposition.
Navigate the three primary zones of the Scratch interface — Stage, Sprite List, and Code Blocks Area — and locate the Events block category.
Configure a new Scratch project by deleting the default Cat sprite, adding the Bat sprite and Blue Sky backdrop, and placing the [When Green Flag Clicked] event block in the script area.
Apply digital asset management protocols by naming the project using the agreed convention (FirstName's Game) and saving via cloud storage or local .sb3 export.

x15: Structured teacher observation during Guided Practice: teacher circulates and visually confirms each student has completed all four mandatory workspace actions (delete Cat, add Bat, add Blue Sky backdrop, place [When Green Flag Clicked] block).
Oral group questioning during the Checking for Understanding phase: teacher poses decomposition and interface questions to groups to gauge readiness before releasing to Guided Practice.

Backup Worksheet (Assessment FOR Learning tool for fast finishers): students label the three Scratch interface zones and write one sentence per zone — teacher collects at exit as a record of initial interface comprehension.

x19: Whether students correctly identify at least three discrete game components (Bat, Crystal, Score) during the oral decomposition activity.
Whether each student has located the Events drawer and placed the [When Green Flag Clicked] block in their script area.
Whether every student has named and saved their Scratch project before the lesson ends.
x20: Oral group questions during the Anticipatory Set and Checking for Understanding phases; listen for computational vocabulary; note any student unable to identify more than one component for Lesson 2 follow-up.
Physical circulation during Guided Practice; visually inspect each screen to confirm Bat sprite presence and green flag block placement.
Final visual scan of all student screens during the Conclusion; verbally prompt any student whose project is unnamed or unsaved.

x21: Basic ICT proficiency: ability to log in to a school account, open and navigate a web browser to a specified URL, and operate a mouse or trackpad.
General file management awareness: understanding that digital work must be saved to prevent data loss, analogous to saving a Word document.
Implicit event-driven logic from everyday experience: awareness that a button press triggers an action (e.g., pressing play starts a video), which bridges to the [When Green Flag Clicked] concept.
Foundational familiarity with computer games as rule-based systems with characters, an objective, and a score — no prior Scratch or coding experience is assumed.

x22: Student devices (school-issued laptops or tablets) with internet access and Chrome browser
Projector connected to teacher display device
Pre-prepared WALT/WILF slide displayed on the projector screen at lesson start
Teacher-prepared demo link: the fully featured 'Catch the Crystal' Scratch project (including bomb and speed-up features) — for display only
Scratch accounts (pre-registered with school email, or students register on arrival)
Backup Worksheet: printed A4 diagram of the Scratch interface with five labelled arrows and blank boxes for zone name and one-sentence description (one per student)
Whiteboard and markers for recording decomposition components

x24: <o>Open the 'Catch the Crystal' demo on the projector in full-screen mode</o> before students enter; let the complete game — including bomb drops and speed-up — play silently as students settle.

Pose decomposition questions to the class in small groups (apply wait time; not to individuals): <y>Look at everything moving on screen. Can you name the separate, independent things you can see?</y> <y>What exact rule makes the score go up — what has to happen?</y> <y>If you had to build this from nothing, what would be the very first piece?</y>

<o>Record student responses on the whiteboard in three labelled columns</o>, narrowing the discussion until the class agrees on the three Base Game components: Bat (player sprite), Crystal (falling sprite), Score (variable).

Set the scope boundary: <y>Today we are only building these three pieces. Everything else you saw — the bomb, the speed-up — those are challenges we will choose from later. For now, simple and solid.</y>
part1.x25: Madeline Hunter Step — Anticipatory Set The demo game plays before the lesson formally opens, connecting students' prior gaming experience to today's design task. The oral decomposition activity operationalises Decomposition as a computational thinking strategy. Do not deliver WALT/WILF until Part 2.

part2.x27: Madeline Hunter Step — Objective and Purpose This lesson is grounded in constructivist theory: students actively construct understanding by observing a complex system, identifying its components, and building upon prior knowledge of digital tools. Take the roll quietly while the WALT/WILF slide is displayed on the projector. Read WALT aloud: We are learning to: break a digital game into its key parts, set up our Scratch workspace, and save our work correctly. Read WILF aloud: What I am looking for: you can name at least three separate parts of a game, find the right blocks in Scratch, and have your project saved and named by the end of today.
part2.x28: <u><bl>Decomposition focus questions (posed in Part 1 to groups, not individuals):</bl></u> || ["•", "What are the separate, independent moving things on the screen?", "What exact rule must be satisfied for the score to increase?", "If you could only keep one element and the game must still make sense, which would it be and why?"]

part1.x33: Madeline Hunter Step — Input Instructional Input — Scratch Interface Orientation Direct students to open Chrome and navigate to scratch.mit.edu; log in or create a Scratch account. Display the Scratch interface on the projector and use a pointer to label each of the three zones: Zone 1 — The Stage: this is where your game will actually run. Think of it as the screen your player will look at. Zone 2 — The Sprite List: this is your cast of characters. Every moving thing in your game lives here as a sprite. Zone 3 — The Code Blocks Area: this is your instruction toolbox. You snap coloured blocks together here to build your game's brain.
part1.x34: EAL/D and visual learner support: use the projector pointer to physically highlight each zone as it is named — do not rely on verbal description alone. Content boundary: do not introduce X/Y coordinates, loops, or any block categories beyond the Events drawer at this stage.

part2.x36: Madeline Hunter Step — Modeling Teacher Demonstration — All Workspace Setup Steps (students observe the projector only; do not touch devices yet) Step 1 — Delete the default Cat sprite: Right-click directly on the Cat icon in the Sprite List at the bottom right. A small menu will appear — select Delete. Your stage should now be completely empty. Step 2 — Add the Bat sprite: See the blue circle with a small cat face at the bottom right of the Sprite List? Click it. In the library that opens, type Bat into the search box. Click the Bat thumbnail. A Bat should appear on your Stage. Step 3 — Add the Blue Sky backdrop: Look at the very bottom right of the screen — there is a small landscape icon next to the word Stage. Click it. Search for Blue Sky and click it. Your stage background should now be blue. Step 4 — Place the [When Green Flag Clicked] block: Find the yellow Events category — it looks like a lightning bolt. Drag the [When Green Flag Clicked] block onto the blank script area. That block is your game's ignition switch.
part2.x37:
<r>Students observe the full demonstration before touching their own devices — this is the complete Modeling phase.</r>

<u>Common errors to intercept during Guided Practice:</u> || ["-", "Student adds a backdrop via the Paint option — redirect to the library search tab.", "Student cannot find Bat — confirm correct spelling with no trailing characters.", "Student accidentally deletes the wrong sprite — undo with Ctrl+Z or re-add from library."] || <r>If a device fails to load Scratch, temporarily pair the student with a neighbour; do not halt the class.</r>

part3.x39: Madeline Hunter Step — Checking for Understanding Before releasing students to Guided Practice, pose the following questions to small groups (apply wait time; not to individuals): Point to where on the Scratch screen you would find the Events drawer. What colour is it? If I asked you to delete the Cat sprite right now, what would you click first? What is the name of the block that starts your program when you click the green flag? Scan the room for hesitation or confusion. If more than one-third of the class cannot answer confidently, repeat the relevant step of the Modeling demonstration before proceeding.
part3.x40: Gate check: Only proceed to Guided Practice once the class demonstrates sufficient readiness. Checking for Understanding is the decision point, not a formality. If necessary, re-demonstrate and re-check before releasing to practice.

part4.x42: Madeline Hunter Step — Guided Practice Students replicate all four workspace setup steps on their own devices. Steps are issued one at a time (Gradual Release of Responsibility — We do it). Step 1: Right-click the Cat icon in the Sprite List → select Delete. Stage should now be empty. Pause and confirm all students have an empty stage before proceeding. Step 2: Click the blue circle at the bottom right of the Sprite List → type Bat → click the Bat thumbnail. Circulate and confirm Bat is visible on all student stages. Step 3: Click the landscape icon next to the word Stage → search Blue Sky → click it. Circulate and confirm Blue Sky backdrop is applied on all screens. Step 4: Find the yellow Events category → drag [When Green Flag Clicked] onto the blank script area. Circulate and visually confirm all students have the block placed in their script area.
part4.x43:
<u>Differentiation:</u>

Students experiencing difficulty receive direct 1:1 support during teacher circulation. Students who complete all four steps early may visually explore the remaining block categories (without dragging any blocks) and record their predictions about what each colour represents.

Cooperative learning permitted: students who have completed may offer quiet verbal assistance to a neighbour — they may not touch the neighbour's keyboard.

part5.x45: Madeline Hunter Step — Independent Practice Distribute the Backup Worksheet to students who have completed all four mandatory workspace actions. Read task instructions aloud: On your worksheet you will see a Scratch screenshot with five arrows pointing to different areas. For each arrow: write the name of that area, then write one sentence explaining what it does. Here is an example — arrow one points to the Stage. You write: Stage — the area where the game runs and is shown to the player. Use that same format for all five. Teacher continues circulating to provide direct support to students still completing workspace setup.
part5.x46:
<u>Differentiation:</u>

Students still completing setup steps receive direct 1:1 support.

Students who finish the worksheet rapidly may visually explore the remaining block categories (without dragging any blocks) and note their predictions about what each colour represents.

x54: <o>Signal the class to pause their Scratch work and direct attention to the projector.</o>

Demonstrate naming convention: <y>Click the project title at the very top of the screen — it currently says Untitled. Change it to your first name followed by the word Game. For example: Alex's Game.</y>
Demonstrate cloud save: <y>Click File in the top menu bar, then click Save now. Scratch saves your project to your online account.</y>
Demonstrate local backup: <y>Click File again, then Save to your computer. This downloads a .sb3 file to your Downloads folder — keep it as a backup.</y>
<o>Conduct a final visual scan of all student screens</o> to confirm every project is named and saved.
part1.x55:
<u><r>Exit requirement</r></u>

All students must demonstrate a named, saved project before dismissal. Students who completed the Backup Worksheet may place it on the teacher's desk as they leave.

part2.x57: Madeline Hunter Step — Closure Pose the following questions to small groups using wait time (not to individuals): We broke the game into pieces today. What is the name of that thinking skill? What are the three zones of the Scratch screen? Can your group name all three? What is the very first block that every Scratch program must begin with? Briefly acknowledge progress: the three components identified today — Bat, Crystal, and Score — are exactly what we will continue building in our next session. Dismiss students in an orderly manner once all screens show a named and saved project.
part2.x58: Assessment FOR Learning: oral group responses to Closure questions provide immediate formative data on class-wide retention of Decomposition, Stage/Sprite/Events vocabulary, and the [When Green Flag Clicked] trigger block — all foundational to the next lesson.
